# Title
#	Study_Name: Upper Colorado River 1,244 Year Bias Corrected Flow Reconstructions 
#--------------------
# Investigators
#	Investigators: Robeson, S.M.; Maxwell, J.T.; Ficklin, D.L.
#--------------------
# Description_Notes_and_Keywords
#	Description: Quantile mapping applied to the original Meko et al. (2007) reconstruction of Upper Colorado River flow at Lee's Ferry, 
#	Arizona (USA), to better evaluate the magnitude, duration, and intensity of extreme droughts and pluvials in the 1200+ year streamflow record.
#	The reconstruction gives the total flow for each water year (October 1 to September 30, with the yearly designation referring to 
#	the latter calendar year) from 762 to 2005 CE. All observed and reconstructed flows are reported in billions of cubic meters per year. 
#	The reconstructed flow is for "naturalized" streamflow, which is an estimate of flow after removing the impacts of human activity 
#	such as reservoirs, irrigation-water extractions, and other depletions. Naturalized streamflow is used because it represents 
#	interannual climate variability rather than human use of river water. 
#
#	The data files are:
#	1) The original and bias-corrected time series for 762 to 2005 for the four nested models that Meko et al. (2007) used to create the full reconstruction. 
#	2) A text file supplied by Dr. David Meko of the University of Arizona contains the original (unadjusted) time series for the four nested models.
#	3) An R script to perform bias correction on the four nested models that are then composited to create the full bias-corrected time series.
#
#--------------------
# Publication 
#	Authors: Scott M. Robeson, Justin T. Maxwell, Darren L. Ficklin
#	Published_Date_or_Year: 2020-01-16     
#	Published_Title: Bias Correction of Paleoclimatic Reconstructions: A New Look at 1,200+ Years of Upper Colorado River Flow
#	Journal_Name: Geophysical Research Letters
#	Volume: 47
#	Edition: e2019GL086689
#	Issue: 1 
#	Pages: 
#	Report_Number: 
#	DOI: 10.1029/2019GL086689
#	Online_Resource: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2019GL086689
#	Full_Citation: 
#	Abstract: Bias correction, while widely used with climate-model output, is not typically applied to paleoclimatic reconstructions. While many reconstruction models have low average error, they still may contain bias, especially in the tails of distributions. Bias correction, used cautiously, can be a valuable procedure that alters interpretations of past events. Analyzing the iconic tree-ring reconstruction of Upper Colorado River flow, we find that its probability distribution is markedly different from that of observed flow. Using quantile mapping to bias correct the reconstruction, we analyze the full reconstructed record and two events in particular: the 1100s megadrought and the early 1600s pluvial. Overall, bias correction made the 1100s megadrought, the largest in the 1,200+ year record, even more extreme. After bias correction, the early 1600s pluvial marginally exceeds the early twentieth century pluvial in magnitude but not in duration. Overall, bias correction should be considered whenever paleoclimatic reconstructions are compared directly to observations.
